paras: The lynching of William (Bee) Washington took place on the night of Saturday, August 15, 1903, when a party of about seventy-five mounted men hanged a Black man to a tree just inside Mississippi, near the Louisiana line. Washington was accused of killing Stanley Wood, a young white clerk, and was tracked into Louisiana with bloodhounds and a hired river steamer before his capture at Red River Landing. A New Orleans report noted that the sheriff of West Feliciana Parish was present and did not stop it.

According to an Associated Press dispatch from Natchez, Wood, an 18-year-old clerk at the Line Store on the Mississippi-Louisiana line, was shot and killed on Monday, August 10. The New Orleans version placed the killing near Talbert, "immediately on the State line," and said the accused fled into Louisiana and crossed the Mississippi River into Pointe Coupee Parish.

A mob of seventy-five men on horseback with bloodhounds set out after him, and the steamer Betsey Ann was hired to follow his trail. He was traced to Red River Landing, La., and captured there, then taken back a short distance across the state line into Mississippi and hanged to a tree. The Natchez dispatch said he was taken to Tarbert, a river point near the scene of the killing, while a Mississippi news column placed the lynching at Tarbert, near Red River Landing.

The New Orleans report claimed that he confessed to the killing but said he had been drunk at the time; no other source repeats the confession. The same report said the Sheriff of West Feliciana "was present at the lynching, but was unable to prevent it."

The Natchez dispatch added that a posse was pursuing several Black men accused of supplying Washington with money, clothes and provisions; the coverage does not show what became of them. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers first through the AP Natchez dispatch of August 15, which Southern and Northern papers printed the next day with the lynching only "reported." Headline writers nonetheless treated the accusation as proven, from "Murderer Was Lynched" in Pine Bluff and "Murderer Reported Lynched" in Savannah to "Bee of the Bloody Hands Hanged" in Raleigh and "A Negro Summarily Dealt With for Killing a Young Clerk" in Bryan, Texas. The Birmingham Age-Herald headed it "Another Negro Lynched" and called the accused "a burly negro."

A separate New Orleans dispatch, carried by the New York Sun and the Washington Times on August 17, supplied the mob's size, the bloodhounds, the steamer and the sheriff's presence, under the Sun's headline "Sheriff Saw Him Hanged." Weekly news digests in Middleburgh, Pa., Canton, Miss., and Newport reduced the case to a single line, and Mississippi's own state column ran it among routine items such as charters and deaths. In San Juan, the Boletin Mercantil retold it in Spanish under "Otro lynchamiento," stressing that he was lynched "sin mas ceremonia" before an authority that did nothing.
All of the coverage located came from the white press; no account in the Black press was found.

The victim's name appears as William Washington in the New Orleans dispatch and the Boletin, as Bee Washington in the Natchez dispatch and digests, and as B. or B. E. Washington in Birmingham and Mississippi. The Age-Herald gave Wood's age as 16 against 18 elsewhere, and the New Orleans report spelled his name Woods.

The timing is also uneven: the Natchez dispatch dated August 15 already called him "reported" lynched, while the New Orleans versions placed the hanging on Saturday night, August 15, and a Pennsylvania digest listed it under Monday, August 17.

reader.title: Lynching of William (Bee) Washington
bases: A mob or posse of about seventy-five men tracked a Black man accused of killing a white clerk, captured him at Red River Landing and hanged him to a tree (A1, A9, A12).

The New Orleans report states that seventy-five mounted men captured Washington and hanged him to a tree with no legal process, for the killing of Stanley Woods (A9, A10); the AP Natchez report and a Mississippi column independently report the capture by a posse and the lynching (A1, A12).

The AP Natchez dispatch (A1, A2, A5), the separate New Orleans dispatch (A9, A10) and a Mississippi state news column (A12) agree on the capture at Red River Landing and the lynching, though the first Natchez report called the lynching only 'reported'.

accounts.label: AP Natchez dispatch
accounts.gist: Bee Washington, who killed clerk Stanley Wood, was captured by a posse at Red River Landing and taken to Tarbert near the scene, where 'it is reported' he was lynched; a posse was pursuing Black men who had helped him.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: William Washington fled into Pointe Coupee Parish, was tracked by seventy-five mounted men with bloodhounds and a hired steamer, captured at Red River Landing and hanged in Mississippi with the West Feliciana sheriff present; it says he confessed but said he was drunk.

accounts.label: Mississippi state column
accounts.gist: B. E. Washington, who shot Stanley Wood, 18, on the state line, was lynched at Tarbert, near Red River Landing.

framing.detail: Southern papers ran the AP text under headlines that treated the accusation as settled: 'Murderer Was Lynched', 'Murderer Reported Lynched', 'Bee of the Bloody Hands Hanged', 'A Negro Summarily Dealt With for Killing a Young Clerk'.
The New York Sun headlined the New Orleans story 'NEGRO LYNCHED FOR MURDER' with 'Sheriff Saw Him Hanged', reporting the sheriff's presence without comment.
The Boletin Mercantil, under 'Otro lynchamiento', noted that he was lynched 'sin mas ceremonia' before an authority that did nothing and added an exclamation at the use of dogs.
